A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same noise-optimization framework despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figures 1–4 report original numerical evaluations of optimized noise distributions and their privacy guarantees.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original numerical evaluations, including additional mechanism comparisons and repeated-seed MSE experiments on three datasets.

M1.justification: The distribution families, geometric tails, RDP optimization objective, initialization, preconditioned gradient descent, and alpha updates remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–3 specify the same procedures.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates noise distributions without real-data query experiments. V2 adds private statistical queries on Breast Cancer Wisconsin Diagnostic, Diabetes, and UCI Heart Disease Cleveland data, covering feature averages and subgroup-specific clinical statistics.

E2.justification: Cactus and Staircase were discussed but not evaluated as comparators in v1. V2 adds them to the privacy curves and composition grid, including discrete counterparts in Figures 5 and 7, and directly compares distribution shapes in Figure 2. The new dataset table reports comparisons against Gaussian.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a dataset protocol using percentile normalization, clipping, ten queries, and 100,000 noisy outputs per query, measuring MSE at fixed privacy budgets. Figure 1 changes its standard deviation from 5 to 8. The earlier standard-deviation-5 pointwise comparison remains in Appendix D, alongside additional parameter settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct numerical checks of Cactus recovery at 50,000 compositions and Staircase recovery at one composition in Figure 2. It also expands distribution-shape examples and adds a delta = 10^-9 composition grid in Appendix D, substantially extending the earlier parameter and regime analyses.

E5.justification: V2 introduces mean and standard deviation reporting across 20 random seeds for the new MSE experiments in Table 1. V1 contains no comparable uncertainty reporting. This addition does not establish any increase in runs for the retained numerical evaluations.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds mean MSE reductions of 8.11–11.48% against Gaussian, alongside new distribution-recovery results and broader comparator rankings. Figure 1 changes the reported optimized epsilon from 2.66 to 1.62, but also changes standard deviation from 5 to 8; these are different-setting results.

T1.justification: The mathematical framework, Theorems 3.1 and 3.6, Proposition 3.5, and proofs in Appendices A–C are unchanged. Equation 1 merely abbreviates the expectation notation; the added experiments do not introduce new theoretical results.

C1.justification: The abstract, conclusion, and central framework and endpoint-recovery claims remain unchanged. The introductory performance illustration broadens its lower-epsilon claim from Gaussian and Laplace to the enlarged comparator set including Cactus and Staircase.

C2.justification: V2 expands the mechanism-selection interpretation, presenting optimized noise as a reliable default when the best conventional mechanism is unclear. Appendix D explains how noise scale shifts the improvement region and explicitly limits the dataset comparison to noise addition, excluding the shared quantile-release privacy cost.

D1.justification: V2 adds an implementation repository reference and substantial experimental documentation in Appendix D: dataset sizes and features, query descriptions, percentile rescaling, clipping, and sampling procedures. New distribution examples also specify their numerical parameters. These additions improve documentation without changing the core algorithm.

R1.justification: The existing methodological references are retained, while dataset sources and an implementation reference are added. Cactus and Staircase receive more explicit positioning as practical alternatives, although their previously stated optimality regimes and the paper's methodological novelty remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The title changes to 'Optimizing Noise Distributions for Differential Privacy.' V2 rewrites and expands the numerical discussion and adds Appendix D, acknowledgements, and an impact statement. The main section sequence, methodological exposition, and proof text remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The visual presentation is extensively revised: comparison plots gain curves and legends, the composition grid gains additional mechanism categories, and new paired distribution plots and an MSE table appear. V1's Figure 3 comparison is retained and expanded as v2's appendix Figure 7; the original single-distribution illustration is replaced by other examples.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation by addressing v1's omission of Cactus and Staircase from evaluated baselines and directly testing the claimed recovery of these mechanisms. It also adds dataset utility experiments with uncertainty reporting and reproduction details while preserving the theory. The dataset results exclude quantile-release privacy costs, limiting their interpretation to relative noise-mechanism utility, but the broader comparative evidence provides a substantial overall improvement.
